title: In Psalterium Expositio
author: Cassiodorus
source: Translated by Claude from tmp1184.tmp1184.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Invitavit autem cum dixit : Beatus vir, et reliqua; deterruit autem cum ait : Non sic impii, non sic, etc. Efficacis- simum plane doctrinae genus, et invitare prosperis, et terrere contrariis; sicut et Pater Augustinus in libris de Doctrina Christiana memorat dicens (Lib. IV, cap. 4) : Debet igitur divinarum Scripturarum tractator et doctor, defensor rectae fidei, ac debella- tor erroris, et bona docere, et mala dedocere. Quod institutionis genus et in decimo quarto, et in trice- simo sexto, et in centesimo decimo, et in centesimo decimo octavo psalmo potenter exsequitur, ut distin- ctio sit in comminatione supplicii, magnitudo sem- per in praemiis.
passages.english: He invited when he said: "Blessed is the man," and the rest; and he deterred when he said: "Not so the wicked, not so," etc. This is plainly a most effective kind of teaching, both to invite by prosperous things and to frighten by their opposites; as Father Augustine too records in his books On Christian Doctrine, saying (Book IV, ch. 4): "The interpreter and teacher of the divine Scriptures, the defender of right faith and the vanquisher of error, ought therefore both to teach what is good and to unteach what is bad." This kind of instruction is powerfully carried out in the fourteenth, the thirty-sixth, the hundred and tenth and the hundred and eighteenth psalms, so that there is measure in the threat of punishment, but always greatness in the rewards.
passages.notes: "distinctio" here seems to mean restraint or measured discrimination in threatening punishment, as opposed to lavishness in rewards; the sense is somewhat uncertain.

passages.original: Et ne per haereticas contentiones Christiani animus fluctuet, quem oportet omnia ve- raciter fixeque credere, nominis ipsius definitionem auctoritate Patrum brevi satisfactione concludimus. Audiamus ergo beatum ac doctissimum Augustinum in evangelistae Joannis expositione dicentem (Tract. 78, in Joan.) : Agnoscamus geminam substantiam Christi, divinam scilicet, qua aequalis est Patri; hu- manam, qua major est Pater; utrumque autem simul, non duo, sed unus est Christus, ne sit quaternitas, non Trinitas Deus; ac per hoc Christus est Deus, anima rationalis, et caro. Qua veritate recognita, competenter mortiferos vitamus errores.
passages.english: And so that the mind of a Christian, who ought to believe all things truly and firmly, may not waver through heretical disputes, we conclude the definition of that very name with a brief satisfaction from the authority of the Fathers. Let us hear, then, the blessed and most learned Augustine, saying in his exposition of the evangelist John (Tractate 78 on John): "Let us acknowledge the twofold substance of Christ: the divine, namely, by which he is equal to the Father; the human, by which the Father is greater; yet both together are not two, but one Christ, lest God be a quaternity and not a Trinity; and thus Christ is God, a rational soul, and flesh." Once this truth is recognized, we fittingly avoid deadly errors.

passages.original: Et ideo psalmus hic omni convenit Christiano, qui amore Domini flamma Dominicae duritatis accenditur, sine qua totum abje- ctum est quidquid in humanis rebus putatur exi- mium. De qua re hic primus est psalmus, quem octogesimus tertius, et octogesimus quartus subse- quuntur. Sed in his nominibus illud meminisse de- bemus quod beatus Hieronymus ait (In Expos. tituli psal. LXXXIV), omne psalterium sagaci mente per- lustrans. Nunquam invenio quod filii Core aliquid triste cantaverint : semper enim in psalmis eorum laeta sunt et jucunda; saecularibusque contemptis coelestia et aeterna desiderant, congruentes interpre- tationi nominis sui.
passages.english: And therefore this psalm suits every Christian who, through love of the Lord, is set alight by the flame of the Lord's hardness, without which whatever is thought outstanding in human affairs is entirely worthless. On this subject this is the first psalm, and the eighty-third and eighty-fourth follow it. But regarding these names we ought to remember what blessed Jerome says (in his exposition of the title of Psalm 84), surveying the whole Psalter with a keen mind: "I never find that the sons of Korah sang anything sad: for in their psalms things are always glad and joyful; and, despising worldly things, they desire heavenly and eternal ones, in keeping with the interpretation of their name."
passages.notes: "Dominicae duritatis" ("the Lord's hardness") is odd; perhaps a corruption (e.g. for "caritatis", "of the Lord's love").

passages.original: Non quia forma ejus decore lactei coloris eluxit, aut flavo crine lampavit, aut insigni statura praeminuit; sed veraciter humano genere pulchrior fuit, quia peccata non habuit. Illud enim recte speciosum dicitur, quod gratia mundissi- mae puritatis ornatur; quamvis Pater Augustinus speciem corporis ejus dicat fuisse laudabilem. Sed exemplum Isaiae supra positum ad passionis ejus re- tulit tempus quando et colaphis caesus, et spinis co- ronatus, et sputis legitur esse complutus. Ecclesia vero quae Domini Salvatoris portat 151, imaginem sic legitur in Canticis canticorum : Fusca sum et decora (Cant.
passages.english: Not because his form shone with the beauty of a milk-white complexion, or gleamed with golden hair, or stood out by remarkable stature; but he was truly more beautiful than the human race because he had no sins. For that is rightly called beautiful which is adorned with the grace of the purest purity; although Father Augustine says that the appearance of his body was praiseworthy. But he referred the passage of Isaiah quoted above to the time of his passion, when he is read to have been both struck with blows, and crowned with thorns, and drenched with spittle. The Church, however, which bears the image of the Lord Saviour, is thus read of in the Song of Songs: "I am dark and comely" (Song
passages.notes: "151" is a page number of the printed edition, omitted. The reference is completed in the following context (I, 4).

passages.original: Pasti sumus, o bone Rex, convivio nuptiali delicias coelestes haurientes. Praesta nobis, Sponse mirabilis, ut qui hic spe laetati sumus, in futuro perfectissimo gaudio compleamur. Hunc etiam psalmum et beatus Hieronymus ad Priu- cipiam virginem scribens (Epist. 140), mirabili (ut assolet) nitore tractavit. Quem ideo commemoran- dum esse putavimus; ut quod a nobis minus for- tasse declaratum est, illius viri doctissimi explana- tionibus suppleatur.
passages.english: We have been fed, O good King, at the wedding feast, drinking in heavenly delights. Grant us, wonderful Bridegroom, that we who here have rejoiced in hope may in the future be filled with most perfect joy. Blessed Jerome too, writing to the virgin Principia (Letter 140), treated this psalm with wonderful brilliance, as is his custom. We thought, therefore, that he should be mentioned, so that what has perhaps been less clearly explained by us may be supplied by the explanations of that most learned man.

passages.original: Venit ad secundum docendi modum, ubi peccatores cum sapientibus hujus mundi dicit esse perituros, et divitias suas, quas magnopere dilige- bant, non suis, sed, quod gravius ureret, extraneis successoribus definit esse relinquendas; ut propter quas omnia peccata commiserant, non possessione ipsarum, nec proprio successore laetarentur; sicut Salomon dicit : In quod peccaverunt, nec laetari [ed., latere ] potuerunt (Sap.X, 8). Cum viderit peccator utique sapientes saeculi istius ab interitu non liberari, ut fuit Solon Atheniensis, Philo Lacedaemonius, Ari- stippus, et caeteri qui mundanae sapientiae celeberrima laude viguerunt; sed videt eos communiter mori, quos divinae Sapientiae participes aestimabat. Sequi- tur, simul insipiens et stultus peribunt.
passages.english: He comes to the second mode of teaching, where he says that sinners will perish together with the wise of this world, and he declares that their riches, which they loved so greatly, must be left not to their own [heirs] but, what would burn more painfully, to strange successors; so that they might take no joy either in the possession of the very things for whose sake they had committed every sin, or in a successor of their own. As Solomon says: "In that wherein they sinned, they could not even rejoice" (Wisdom 10:8). When the sinner sees that the wise of this world are certainly not freed from death, such as Solon the Athenian, Philo the Lacedaemonian, Aristippus, and the others who flourished with the most celebrated praise for worldly wisdom, he sees instead that those whom he reckoned sharers in divine Wisdom die in common [with all]. There follows: "the foolish and the senseless shall perish together."
passages.notes: The edition notes a variant: 'laetari' (rejoice) is printed, with 'latere' (lie hidden) reported as the reading of another edition. 'Philo Lacedaemonius' is not readily identifiable; possibly a corruption for Chilon of Sparta, one of the Seven Sages. 'Cum viderit... sed videt' is grammatically loose in the Latin; rendered as a single sentence.

passages.original: Dicit enim sententiam frequenter iteratam : Verum- tamen vani filii hominum, ut vitium suum cognoscens humanitas, ad auctorem salutis atque veritatis celerri- ma supplicatione festinet. Sic enim in trigesimo octavo psalmo dictum est : Verumtamen universa vanitas omnis homo vivens (Psal. XXXVIII, 6). Quod et Sapiens ille frequenter repetit dicens : Omnia vanitas vanita- tum (Eccle. I, 2). Nonnullos autem movere solet, cur et in Psalmis legatur : Vani filii hominum; et in Sa- lomone : Universa vanitas (Ibid., 14)? Nunquid coe- lestia et terrestria, quae Deus creavit, et omnia valde bona, cuncta in vanitate consistunt? Non utique, sed comparata potioribus illa minora nimis et inania ju- dicantur; sicut ait beatus Hieronymus : Luceria lampadis comparatione pro nihilo stellae comparatione non lucet; stellam lunae confer, et caeca est; lunam soli junge, non rutilat; solem Christo confer, et tenebrae sunt. Sic omnia vana fiunt, quae dum melioribus comparantur, fulgore proprio mi- (??) tur. Sic homines, cum ad comparationem su- pernae veritatis veniunt, ut vani rationabiliter esse dicamur. Sed huic rei addidit vilium quo maxime laborat humanitas.
passages.english: For he states a sentence often repeated: "But vain are the sons of men," so that humanity, recognizing its fault, may hasten with swiftest supplication to the author of salvation and truth. For thus it was said in the thirty-eighth psalm: "But every living man is altogether vanity" (Ps. 38:6). This too that Wise Man often repeats, saying: "All is vanity of vanities" (Eccles. 1:2). Some, however, are usually troubled as to why it is read both in the Psalms, "Vain are the sons of men," and in Solomon, "All is vanity" (ibid., 14). Do the heavenly and earthly things which God created, all very good, all consist in vanity? Certainly not; but when compared with greater things, these lesser ones are judged very small and empty; as blessed Jerome says: "A lamp's light, by comparison with a lamp [it is something]; by comparison with a star it is as nothing and does not shine; compare a star with the moon, and it is blind; set the moon beside the sun, it does not glow; compare the sun with Christ, and it is darkness." So all things become vain which, when compared with better things, are diminished in their own brightness. So with men: when they come to comparison with the heavenly truth, we are reasonably said to be vain. But to this matter he added the vice from which humanity chiefly suffers.
passages.notes: The Jerome quotation is garbled ("Luceria lampadis comparatione pro nihilo stellae comparatione non lucet"); probably something like "a lantern compared with a lamp is as nothing; compared with a star it does not shine"; rendered tentatively. "mi- (??) tur" read as "minuuntur" (are diminished). "vilium" read as "vitium" (vice).

passages.original: Qui malignatus est in locis sanctis ejus, quando sacer- dotes lotaque ministeria 250 templi in praedam missa patuerunt, cunctaque gens Hebraeorum aut gladio subjacuit, aut captivitati subjugata servivit. Hoc enim nimis acerrimum bellum Josephi Historia septem libris celebrata describit.
passages.english: "Who has done evil in his holy places": when the priests and the washed vessels of the temple lay exposed, given over as plunder, and the whole Hebrew nation either fell beneath the sword or, subjugated by captivity, served as slaves. For this most bitter war is described by the History of Josephus, celebrated in seven books.
passages.notes: "lotaque ministeria" ("washed vessels/services") is odd; perhaps corrupt for "totaque ministeria" ("all the services"). "250" is a page number, omitted.

passages.original: quae vero fidei nostrae possunt indi- care notitiam, spirituali intellectu (sicut a majoribus accepimus) explanabimus. Unde solliciti esse debe- mus, paratique ad audiendum : quia ipse quoque vir eloquentissimus Pater Augustinus hunc psalmum et sedule dicit perquirendum, et de eodem laboriosis- sime disputandum.
passages.english: but what can point to knowledge of our faith we shall explain by a spiritual understanding, as we have received from our elders. Therefore we ought to be attentive and ready to listen, because that most eloquent man, Father Augustine, also says that this psalm must be both diligently searched out and discussed with the greatest labour.

passages.original: Deinde congruum fuit ut rem nolam varia relatione descri- beret, cum AEgyptiorum poenas, et totidem Hebraeo- rum beneficia praedicaret. Sic non diversum, sed causa varietatis videtur esse pulcherrimum. Sive (ut Patri Augustino placet) libera est laudatio a lege patrantis : nam qui texit historiam, necesse habet omnia commemorare plenissime; qui vero laudat, pauca de plurimis tetigisse sufficiet. Breviter ergo priora dicit, quia non hic nescientes docet, sed com- memorat utique retinentes.
passages.english: Next, it was fitting that he should describe a known matter with varied narration, since he was proclaiming the punishments of the Egyptians and as many benefits to the Hebrews. Thus it seems not discordant but, because of the variety, most beautiful. Or, as Father Augustine holds, praise is free from the law of one who narrates events: for whoever weaves a history must record everything most fully, but for one who praises it will suffice to have touched on a few things out of many. So he speaks briefly of earlier things, because here he is not teaching the ignorant, but reminding those who certainly remember.
passages.notes: "nolam" read as "notam" (known). "lege patrantis" is unclear; possibly corrupt for "lege narrantis" (the law of one narrating); rendered accordingly.

passages.original: Vers. 9. Moab olla spe mei. In Idumaeam extendam calceamentum meum : mihi allophyli subditi sunt. Moab, sicut Hieronymo placet, significat ex patre, quod est sine patre. Unde diabolum vult intelligi, qui malis operationibus Deum non habet patrem, sed justum judicem. Iste ergo ollae comparatur, quae carnes susceptas decoquit, et in quamdam suavitatem fervido vapore perducit;
passages.english: Verse 9. "Moab is the pot of my hope. Into Idumaea I will stretch out my shoe: the foreigners are made subject to me." Moab, as Jerome holds, means "from the father," that is, without a father. Hence he wants the devil to be understood, who by his evil works has God not as father but as just judge. He, then, is compared to a pot, which cooks the meat put into it and by its boiling steam brings it to a certain tenderness;
passages.notes: The explanation "from the father, that is, without a father" appears paradoxical in the text as given.

passages.original: Nam sicut superiores psalmi alphabetodes quasdam litteras mi- nus habentes, illos designant qui non adeo universis meritis repleti sunt, sed tamen in sancto concilio habitare noscuntur, ita et isti, completis litteris om- nibus, excellentium merita videntur indicare justo- rum. Est et alia causa, ut Pater Hilarius dicit (Pro- log. in Psal.), positi hujus alphabeti : Scimus parvulos et rudes per litteras erudiri, ut sapientiae praecepta conquirant; sic hujusmodi psalmi pueris et incipien- tibus dantur, ut primordia eorum quasi quibusdam elementis docentibus instruantur.
passages.english: For just as the earlier alphabetic psalms, lacking certain letters, signify those who are not so filled with all merits but are nevertheless known to dwell in the holy council, so these too, with all the letters complete, seem to indicate the merits of the outstanding righteous. There is also another reason, as Father Hilary says (Prologue on the Psalms), for this alphabet being set down: we know that little children and beginners are educated through letters, so that they may acquire the precepts of wisdom; so psalms of this kind are given to children and beginners, so that their first steps may be instructed as if by certain elements teaching them.

passages.original: Vers. 3. HE, VAU. Confessio et magnificentia opus ejus, et justitia ejus manet in saeculum saeculi. Opera illa Domini, quae superius dixit, nunc iterum quem- admodum intelligantur exponit. Gloria enim et decor (sicut Pater Hieronymus transtulit) est opus ejus : quoniam et laudabilia sunt nimis, et decora quae fa- cit. Diximus enim Confessionem illam hic accipiendam, quae verbis praeconialibus explicatur. Sequitur, et justitia ejus manet in saeculum saeculi. Hic justitiam Domini, sententiam futuri judicii debemus advertere, quae omnino perpetua est. Justitia quippe ejus manet in saeculum saeculi, cum peccatoribus dixerit : Ite in ignem aeternum, qui paratus est diabolo et angelis ejus (Matth.XXV, 41).
passages.english: Verse 3. HE, VAU. Praise and magnificence are his work, and his justice endures for ever and ever. The works of the Lord which he spoke of above, he now explains again how they are to be understood. For glory and beauty (as Father Jerome translated) is his work, since the things he does are both exceedingly praiseworthy and beautiful. For we have said that 'confession' here is to be taken as that which is set forth in words of proclamation. There follows: and his justice endures for ever and ever. Here by the justice of the Lord we should understand the sentence of the future judgement, which is altogether everlasting. For his justice endures for ever and ever when he says to sinners: Depart into the eternal fire, which was prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt. 25:41).
passages.notes: 'Confessio' is rendered 'praise' in the psalm verse, following Cassiodorus' own explanation that it here means proclamatory praise.

passages.original: Vehementer admiror quoties istum numerum re- perio ingentium sacramentorum honore plenissimum. Ipse enim calculus apostolos complectitur; ipse Israeliticum populum divisit in tribubus, futuram il- lam, sicut Pater Hieronymus ait(In cap.XXXIEzech.), significans beatitud nem duodenaria quantitate distin- gui. Verbi gratia, ut primum locum habeant apo- stoli, secundum prophetae, tertium martyres, quar- tum infantes post baptismum rapti, quintum virgi- nes, sextum recte poenitentes; ut sic usque ad duodecim partes per diversas meritorum distantias gradiatur. Hoc tangere videtur Apostolus cum dicit : Alia claritas solis, alia claritas lunae, alia claritas stellarum (I Cor.XV, 41); et alibi : Stilla a stella differt in claritate : sic erit et resurrectio mortuorum. 386 Quapropter iste psalmus post centesimum duodenario numero constitutus, futurae nobis bea- titudinis imaginem compromittit, quando ad illam aeternae laetitiae similitudinem jugiter Dominum a pueris praecipit esse laudandum.
passages.english: I marvel greatly whenever I find this number most full of the honour of mighty mysteries. For this very count embraces the apostles; it divided the people of Israel into tribes, signifying, as Father Jerome says (On Ezekiel ch. 31), that the future blessedness is distinguished in a twelvefold quantity. For example, that the apostles should hold the first place, the prophets the second, the martyrs the third, infants taken away after baptism the fourth, virgins the fifth, the rightly penitent the sixth; so that it proceeds thus up to twelve parts through various differences of merit. The Apostle seems to touch on this when he says: One is the brightness of the sun, another the brightness of the moon, another the brightness of the stars (1 Cor. 15:41); and elsewhere: Star differs from star in brightness; so also will be the resurrection of the dead. Therefore this psalm, placed at the twelfth number after the hundredth, promises us an image of future blessedness, when it commands that the Lord be praised continually by children, after the likeness of that eternal joy.
passages.notes: 'Stilla' read as 'stella' (scanning error). '386' is a page number, omitted.

passages.original: Quod nos dicimus et divisionis causa positum, et ut perfectum numerum possit in- dicare justorum. Istis enim litteris et Hebraea sapien- tia discitur, et divinorum librorum sacratus numerus continetur. Has enim litteras significationes suas ha- bere (beato Hieronymo testante) cognovimus, quod nunc repetere videtur esse superfluum, cum sit jam alterius labore collectum. Hunc autem psalmum et centesimum quadragesimum quartum, et Deuteronomii canticum Josephus refert elegiaco metro esse com- positos.
passages.english: This we say was set down both for the sake of division and so that it might indicate the perfect number of the righteous. For by these letters Hebrew wisdom is learned, and the sacred number of the divine books is contained. For we know (as blessed Jerome testifies) that these letters have their own meanings, which it seems superfluous to repeat now, since it has already been collected by another's labour. Josephus reports that this psalm and the hundred and forty-fourth, and the song of Deuteronomy, were composed in elegiac metre.

passages.original: Si ad litteram hunc numerum velimus advertere, septem illas significat vices qui- bus se monachorum pia devotio consolatur, id est matutinis, tertia, sexta, nona, lucernaria, comple- toriis, nocturnis. Hoc et sancti Ambrosii hymnus in sextae horae decantatione testatur. Si vero spirituali- ter intendas, continuationem magis dictam sapienter advertis, ut est illud : Benedicam Dominum in omni tempore : semper laus ejus in ore meo (Psal.XXXIII, 2). Sic est etiam hebdomas, quae in hoc semper nu- mero revoluta, longissimum nobis tempus extendit, dum hoc numero clauditur quidquid in mundi istius aetate versatur. Nam et ibi pro infinito ponitur, ubi ait : Septies cadit justus, et resurgit (Prov.XXIV, 16);
passages.english: If we wish to consider this number literally, it signifies those seven times at which the pious devotion of monks consoles itself, that is, at matins, terce, sext, none, the lamp-lighting office, compline, and nocturns. The hymn of Saint Ambrose sung at the sixth hour also bears witness to this. But if you look at it spiritually, you will wisely perceive that continuity is rather what is meant, as in this: I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise is always in my mouth (Ps. 33:2). So too is the week, which, always revolving in this number, extends for us the longest time, since whatever passes in the age of this world is enclosed by this number. For it is also used for the infinite where it says: Seven times the righteous man falls, and rises again (Prov. 24:16);

passages.original: Nam Josephus in libro tertio Antiquitatum ti- tulo octavo, magnarum rerum exinde sacramenta patefecit : probans quatuor colores earum, id est, byssum, purpuram, hyacinthum et coccum, elementa mundi rationabiliter indicasse. Hieronymus etiam ad Fabiolam scribens (Epist. 128), et de hac quoque re non destitit esse proficuus.
passages.english: For Josephus, in the third book of the Antiquities, in the eighth chapter, disclosed from this the mysteries of great matters, proving that their four colours, that is, fine linen, purple, blue and scarlet, reasonably indicated the elements of the world. Jerome too, writing to Fabiola (Letter 128), did not fail to be profitable on this matter as well.
passages.notes: 'Their' refers to the priestly vestments discussed in context.

passages.original: Dominus Christus est, juxta quem stantes doctores haeretici, quasi judices po- puli sui subita voracitate merguntur; qui ideo cor- ruunt in profundum, quoniam supra petram stare non eligunt. Nam quid illis prodest juxta soliditatem stare, quando in ipsa fortitudine non videntur insi- stere? Quod verbum Hieronymus translator posuit, et expositor Pater Augustinus secutus est; ut nemo audeat accusare quod talium virorum auctoritate probatum est. Haec enim verbi translatio nimis hae- reticorum videtur designare perfidiam; nam cum baptizent, cum communicent, cum sacras nobiscum litteras legant, dicuntur juxta petram stare, non in petra.
passages.english: [The rock] is the Lord Christ, standing beside whom the heretical teachers, as judges of their people, are swallowed up by a sudden voracity; they fall headlong into the depth because they do not choose to stand upon the rock. For what does it profit them to stand beside the solid [rock], when they are not seen to stand firm upon that very strength? This word the translator Jerome set down, and the expositor Father Augustine followed; so that no one should dare to fault what has been approved by the authority of such men. For this rendering of the word seems very well to designate the faithlessness of heretics; for though they baptise, though they communicate, though they read the sacred writings with us, they are said to stand beside the rock, not on the rock.

passages.original: Ad hunc igitur omnipotentem, sine initio, sine fine, qui universas mundi omnem- que creaturam suam commeat atque replet, sic ta- men ut in scipso ubique sit totus, malos non prae- sentia, sed gratiae suae virtute derelinquens : Quod Pater Augustinus ad Dardanum scribens, latius ex- plicavit (Epist. 57, in resp. ad quaest. 1). Salutariter nos admonet festinare sermo propheticus, dicens : Venite adoremus, et procidamus coram Domino; plo- remus ante Deum (Psal.XCIV, 6). Et ne omnino flu- ctuantes ac trepidi linqueremur, addidit, qui fecit nos; ut cum nos ab ipso creatos esse cognoscimus, facto- rem nostrum fiducialiter exoremus.
passages.english: To this Almighty, then, without beginning, without end, who pervades and fills the whole world and all his creation, yet in such a way that he is wholly everywhere in himself, forsaking the wicked not by his presence but by the power of his grace (which Father Augustine explained at greater length writing to Dardanus, Letter 57, in reply to question 1), the prophetic word salutarily urges us to hasten, saying: Come, let us worship and fall down before the Lord; let us weep before God (Ps. 94:6). And so that we should not be left altogether wavering and fearful, he added, who made us; so that, since we know we were created by him, we may confidently entreat our maker.
passages.notes: 'scipso' read as 'seipso'. The sentence is syntactically loose in the Latin; punctuation adjusted.
